Subject: Performance pilot qualification — recap + immediate asks

Thanks again for the call earlier today — good alignment on the high-level goals. Quick recap and a compact set of asks so we can scope the pilot.

Recap (what you confirmed):
- Target front-door p95 latency: ~120 ms (goal) for single-turn text generation.
- Expected steady-state throughput: ~200 requests/sec during peak windows, spiky bursts to 350 req/s for short periods.
- Concurrent user sessions: ~40–60 active concurrent sessions.
- Streaming: client wants token-streaming for partial results (token flush every ~200ms).

Primary constraints we heard: latency tightness + cost sensitivity. You also mentioned a 6–8 week internal pilot window with a production-like data sample.

Immediate asks from Redwood to Velocity:
1) Please upload a 12–24 hour representative request sample (we have a template attached: pilot-data-sample.csv). Include average prompt length and expected continuation length.
2) Confirm SLO priority: is 120 ms p95 an absolute must or a stretch target?
3) Identify a single representative endpoint/route we should use for the pilot (helps model/quantization selection).

How we'll approach the pilot (high level):
- Baseline: run your sample traffic on our hosted pilot model to measure real p50/p95 and throughput.
- Cost/perf levers we'll exercise: continuous batching (tunable target latency vs batch size), prefix/KV caching for repeated conversation context, two quantization profiles (8-bit and 4-bit where safe), and a model-variant path (smaller/quantized model for bursts + higher accuracy model for sensitive queries).
- Streaming: prototype token-flush frequency and batching windows to meet your ~200ms flush ask while keeping per-token overhead low.

Next steps / timeline:
- Samir/Lena: upload sample data and confirm SLO priority by EOD Friday.
- Redwood (Ben/Karthik): within 48 hours of receiving sample, we'll run an isolated pilot and share an SLO + cost tradeoff spreadsheet (slo-estimates.xlsx).
- Follow-up call to review results: propose Wed 05/28 10:00–10:45 PT.

Attachments: pilot-data-sample.csv (template), high-level pilot checklist.

Thanks — Priya

- The 120 ms p95 is our customer-visible target. If you can show a fallback path that keeps user experience acceptable at higher latencies during burst windows, that would be fine.
- Representative endpoint will be /nlu/assistant/generate — most traffic is single-turn with prompt sizes ~600–900 bytes and expected continuation ~80–150 tokens.

We should also confirm whether KV/prefix caching requires changes to our client (we prefer minimal client-side changes).

Thanks, Samir — received the sample and ran a quick local pass. High level notes and quick numbers (ballpark) so you have something to plan against: 

Baseline assumptions used for these back-of-envelope estimates:
- Model family: medium-sized open model (parameter-equivalent to ~13B), and a quantized 7B variant for burst fallback.
- Average prompt length: 120 tokens; average completion: 110 tokens.

Quick estimates (per 1M tokens generated):
- FP16 medium model (no quantization, efficient CUDA kernels): ~$220–260 / 1M tokens
- 8-bit quantized (INT8/LLM-int8): ~$120–150 / 1M tokens (latency similar at low concurrency)
- 4-bit extreme quant (Q4) with optimized kernels: ~$70–90 / 1M tokens (some quality drop on edge cases)

Latency/throughput levers and impact: 
- Continuous batching: if we target a 25–40 ms batching window we can group short requests into batches of ~8–16 tokens on average; this can improve throughput by ~1.6–2.2x at modest p95 penalty (~+10–30 ms depending on arrival patterns).
- KV/prefix caching: for repeated context across sessions (50% cache hit rate assumed) we can drop average token compute by up to 30–40% and P95 improves significantly; caching is server-side — no client changes required for prefix caching, but session IDs must be stable.
- Model variants & fallback routing: route burst traffic to a smaller quantized model automatically (no client change). We can run canary routing to validate quality.

Streaming specifics: we can flush partial tokens every ~150–250 ms with a small batching window; this requires the client to accept chunked streaming responses (standard SSE/WebSocket/HTTP chunking). If you must avoid client changes, we can emulate streaming by pushing smaller completions from the server but that adds orchestration complexity.

Recommended pilot configuration: 
- 48-hour run on your six-hour sample replay looped to reproduce burst patterns.
- Compare three model paths: FP16 medium (quality baseline), 8-bit quant (sweet spot), Q4 fallback for cost bursts.
- Instrument: token-level latency histograms, per-route cost, cache hit-rate metrics, and end-to-end client perceived latency.

I'll prepare a short SLO vs cost tradeoff sheet and drop it into the Drive link by EOD for Priya/Samir to review.

Attachments: preliminary numbers and a short config snippet (slo-estimates.xlsx).
